Flint SUMMARY: The Coloso Formation is an early Cretaceous conglomerate-dominated molasse sequence in northern Chile. The sequence was deposited rapidly and records the unroofing of granodioritic and andesitic source rocks. Thin sand units throughout the sequence have been studied palaeomagnetically; the results are complex but can be related to the diagenesis of and-zone alluvium. Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) may be normal or reversed but is usually a combination of the two. Isolation of magnetic components by vector analysis of thermal and AF demagnetization data yields both normal and reversed components which are approximately antiparallel and yield an average pole position at 703, 192"E. This is consistent with late Cretaceous data from northern Chile but not with the established apparent polar wander (APW) path for South America. It may indicate late Cretaceous remagnetization but is considered to be more likely an indication that the present APW path assumes no tectonic rotation and that important relative movements have taken place between northern Chile and Argentina. The Lombriz Formation is overlain by shallow-marine Neocomian limestones of the Tableado Formation (formerly the Way Formation). Diagenetic studies of the orebody and associated sediments reveal a number of features characteristic of the shallow burial diagenesis of arid-zone continental sediments (Walker et al. 1978; Turner 1980). These include dissolution and clay replacement of detrital silicate grains and a suite of authigenic minerals including quartz, feldspar, calcite and hematite. In shallow burial diagenesis, reaction between detrital grains and groundwater controls the supply of ions to interstitial pore solutions. Under suitable chemical conditions minerals precipitate as overgrowths, ce- ments or discrete authigenic phases. Detrital framework composition thus exercises an important control on the subsequent diagenesis. In the Coloso Formation sulphide grains and mineralized clasts from the source area have been thoroughly oxidized and replaced by hematite and clearly have been affected by shallow burial diagenesis. As diagenesis progressed detrital titanomagnetites were oxidized post-depositionally and magnetite was converted to maghemite or hema- tite. Many grains (Fig. 9) show compound mineralogy and it is these which can be expected to account for the coexisting normal and reversed directions of magnetization. The fact that the higher blocking temperature components (carried at least partly by hematite) are exclusively reversed polarity suggests that this diagenetic magnetization may have been generated by a discrete phase of oxidation associated with a period of non-deposition which followed deposition of the Upper Coloso Formation (sandstone units). Secondary (i.e. post-diagenetic) magnetizations subsequently may have been acquired, particularly by coarse-grained (multidomain) magnetite which sur- vived diagenetic oxidation. These magnetizations are predominantly normal and could represent viscous components or partial thermal-remanent magnetiza- tions associated with burial and uplift or Andean igneous activity. The Coloso Formation in Antofagasta Province (Fig. 1) is a conglomerate-dominated alluvial fan succes- sion, 1500 m thick, which passes conformably upwards into evaporites, sandstones and conglomerates which in turn are overlain by Lower Cretaceous marine carbon- ates. The stratigraphy of the succession has recently been modified (our unpublished data) and the new scheme is employed here (Figs 1 & 2). The conglomer- ates are generally unstratified and commonly show no internal organization, althotigh crude coarsening or fining-upwards cycles can be recognized locally. Taljaard (1937) gave a comprehensive account of the geology and petrography of the melilite basalts of the southern Cape, and these data are incorporated in a regional summary by Du Toit (1954). The principal occurrences, and the 4 localities sampled in this study, are shown in Figure 1. The basalts sampled at Spiegel River (or Heidelberg) and Robertson (localities 3 and 1) appear to be from relatively isolated, small (approximately 200 m diameter) intrusive plugs. On Sutherland Commage (locality 4) the field relationships are more obscure and it is uncertain whether the outcrops represent sheet-like bodies or a single plug or ring dike (Taljaard, 1937, p. 291). Saltpetrekop (locality 2) is a conspicuous peak about 15 km SE of Sutherland, which is formed by a plug of breccia and tuff. Numerous satellitic pipes and dikes are grouped around this central volcano. Here, trachyte is the most common rock type, but the sequence of intrusion is: olivine melilitite, trachyte, and carbonatite (Mclver & Ferguson, in prep., after de Wet, 1974, unpubl., thesis). One of the satellite pipes, at Matjesfontein west of Saltpetrekop, contains large aggregates or crystals of hornblende, ilmenite and biotite (Du Toit, 1954, p. 425; Mclver & Ferguson, in prep.). No outcrop remains at Matjesfontein, but i

Introduction The mid to late Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic record of the Atlantic-bordering continents may be used to determine the disposition of the tectonic elements related to the later stages of evolution of the Caledonian-Appalachian mountain belts. Of recent interest is the documentation of the extent and movement of displaced terrains within this belt (Kent & Opdyke, 1978, 1979; Van der Voo, French & French, 1979) and, on the larger scale, possible departure of the distribution of the major continental areas from the Bullard, Everett & Smith (1965) and similar reconstructions (Scotese et al. 1979; Van der Voo, 1983). Lefort & Van der Voo (1981) and Van der Voo (1983) outlined a testable hypothesis, based on available palaeomagnetic data, of the disposition of three major tectonic elements that comprised the Old Red Continent. The elements are Laurentia (North America with the Labrador Sea closed), Baltica (Baltic Shield with the Russian Platform) and Armorica (southern Europe). According to this hypoth

Baltica and Armorica then moved northward with respect to North America to the Bullard, Everett & Smith (1965) position during early Carboniferous time along strike slip faults. The driving force of this movement, was-the collision of Gondwanaland with the Old Red Continent. Slivers of continental crust with dimensions of the order of several hundred kilometres that were on the European side of the strike slip lineament(s) but remained attached to North America after the opening of the present Atlantic Ocean are now identified as displaced terrains such as Acadia (Kent & Opdyke, 1978). As argued by Harland (1978), Harland & Wright (1979), and Harland (1980), the idea of sinistral strike slip motion displacing slivers of continental crust during the late stages of the Caledonian orogeny is an attractive hypothesis that explains many aspects of the geology of Spitsbergen. Spitsbergen may be divided into at least three provinces of older rocks which are separated by two major fault zones. The eastern province has strong similarities to central eastern Greenland (Harland, 1978; Harland & Wright, 1979). Cervid teeth are very similar to giraffid teeth; it is possible that some of the dentitions identified in our faunal list as giraffids may prove to be cervid and conversely, some of the teeth identified as cervids in the earlier faunal lists may prove to be giraffids. Definite identification of the dentitions must await a more detailed taxonomic review of all Siwalik Giraffidae and Cervidae. Until then, we are aware of no antlers recorded from the Tatrot section (or elsewhere in Middle Siwalik deposits), whereas antlers and crania with antlers are fairly common in Upper Siwalik deposits. Lydekker's Cervus latidens, based on a right upper molar, is from the Padhri--Hasnot area where we record several dentitions of giraffids. It should be noted that cervids with antlers (e.g., Procervulus and Stephanocemas) are recorded from Miocene deposits in Europe and northern Asia. The sequence of faunal change in Siwalik sediments is of primary import- ance for the correlation of these terrestrial sediments and related geologic events with similar deposits and events in other parts of the world. rn Asia. The sequence of faunal change in Siwalik sediments is of primary import- ance for the correlation of these terrestrial sediments and related geologic events with similar deposits and events in other parts of the world. Paleontol- ogists and stratigraphers have commonly placed the faunal sequence within a framework established by Pilgrim (1913), relating these divisions (Manchar or Kamlial, Chinji, Nagri, Dhok Pathan, Bhandar, Tatrot, Pinjor, and Boulder Conglomerate) to lithologic formations, or biostratigraphic (zones), or time- stratigraphic (stages) units. It is now apparent that these faunal-stratigraphic divisions are fairly reliable for intercontinental correlation but are unreliable for correlation within the Siwaliks. For example, most paleontologists and stratigraphers accept the correlation of Pilgrim's Pinjor fauna with the European Villafranchian or Biharian fauna, but there is little or no agree- ment on where to place the boundary between Pilgrim's Pinjor and Tatrot faunal intervals in the Siwaliks. For this reason, we have avoided (up to now) placing any sites in Pilgrim's Pinjor or Tatrot faunal intervals, but have placed all of them in an independent, calibrated temporal frame of reference, the geomagnetic time scale. stratigraphy and vertebrate paleontology of the Upper Siwalik subgroup of northern Pakistan. Palaeogeogr., Palaeoclimatol., Palaeoecol., 27 : 1--34. Two hundred and fifty three sites consisting of three samples per site were taken from eight separate stratigraphic sections from sediments of the Upper Siwalik subgroup of northern Pakistan. All samples have been partially demagnetized in alternating fields of from 150 to 300 Oe. The sediments are dipping at angles of up to 75 ° in a variety of directions, and the locality mean directions improve significantly after correcting for bedding attitude, providing a statistically significant fold test at the 95% level. The magnetic stratigraphy was obtained based on the statistically significant well- grouped partially demagnetized data. Two prominent bentonitized tufts occur in several sections above and below a prominent reversal of the earth's magnetic field. Radiometric dates of 2.3 + 0.4 m.y.B.P, and 2.5 + 0.4 m.y.B.P, have been obtained by fission track on zircons from these tufts. This allows the magnetic stratigraphy to be correlated to the standard reversal chronology of the Pliocene and Pleistocene. The longest stratigraphic section (1.87 km in thickness) can be shown to span the time between 0.6 m.y.B.P, and 5.5 m.y.B.P

four meters per thousand years for the Rohtas anticline and three meters per thousand years for the Pabhi Hills. The rates of subsidence (i.e., rates of sedimentation) of the various sections are estimated to range from 0.35 m/103 yr to 0.50 m/103 yr. The first occurrence of conglomerate-containing clasts derived from the Himalayan uplift occurs just prior to the Olduvai event at the base of the Pleistocene. INTRODUC~ON The result of the collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian continent can be seen today in the awe-inspiring Himalayan mountain chain. This orogeny is in part recorded in the sediments derived from them and deposited to the south of the mountains in a subsiding foredeep. These sediments, the Neogene and Quaternary Siwalik Group, contain the remains of the vertebrate faunas which lived on the Indian plate during the late Cenozoic. These faunas have been extensively collected and are well-known as the standard land mammal stages of southern Asia. The Siwalik Group has in turn become involved in the continuing orogeny and has become faulted and folded and is now under active erosion, leading to an abundance of excellent exposures available for study. LABORATORY PROCEDURES After the samples were returned from the field, each one was fashioned into a cube nominally 2.5 cm on each side. The samples were then measured on a commercially available spinner magnetometer described by Molyneaux (1971). Almost all samples were easily measurable with NRM intensities ranging between 10 -7 and 10 -S G/cc with the mode located at 10 -6 G/cc. Washakie Basin, Wyoming The Eocene, fluviatile to lacustrine Washakie Formation is the youngest early Tertiary rock unit cropping out in the Washakie Basin of southwestern 343 Wyoming. The Washakie Basin is a synclinal, structural and topographic basin covering an area of approximately 2500 square miles (6500 square kilometers; Roehler, 1973). It is flanked by the Sierra Madre Range to the east, Wamsutter Arch to the north, Rock Springs Uplift to the west, and Cherokee Ridge to the south. Eocene strata in the basin are approximately 8000 ft {2438 m) thick. Surface sections of the Washakie Formation yield a maximum thickness of approximately 3000 ft (914 m), although Roehler (1969) indicated a possible subsurface thickness of 12,300 ft (3749 m) for the formation. Roehler (1973) divided the Washakie Formation into a lower Kinney Rim Member and an upper Adobe Town Member. Investigation of the biostratigraphy, magnetostrati- graphy and radioisotopic chronology of Eocene sequences in Wyoming and California may greatly increase the temporal precision of intracontinental correlations. A multidisciplinary approach is extremely useful in solving problems in paleontology, geology, and other aspects of earth history. A broad perspective and diverse sources of data often contribute information and in- sights essential to the resolution of scientific inquiries. Washakie Basin, Wyoming The Eocene, fluviatile to lacustrine Washakie Formation is the youngest early Tertiary rock unit cropping out in the Washakie Basin of southwestern 343 Wyoming. The Washakie Basin is a synclinal, structural and topographic basin covering an area of approximately 2500 square miles (6500 square kilometers; Roehler, 1973). It is flanked by the Sierra Madre Range to the east, Wamsutter Arch to the north, Rock Springs Uplift to the west, and Cherokee Ridge to the south. Eocene strata in the basin are approximately 8000 ft {2438 m) thick. Surface sections of the Washakie Formation yield a maximum thickness of approximately 3000 ft (914 m), although Roehler (1969) indicated a possible subsurface thickness of 12,300 ft (3749 m) for the formation. Roehler (1973) divided the Washakie Formation into a lower Kinney Rim Member and an upper Adobe Town Member. The faunal succession of this deposit indicates an age ranging from middle Paleocene (Torrejonian) to early Eocene (Clarkforkian). A minimum of three separately oriented paleomagnetic samples were collected from each of 53 sites in the type and one reference section. Depending upon pilot studies and lithology, in the laboratory the paleomagnetic specimens were treated with either AF or thermal demagnetization (at, respectively, a minimum regime of 25 mT or 200° and 400°C), which appeared to isolate the characteristic component of magnetization. The magnetic polarity zonation is predominantly reversed punctuated by several normal intervals. Based on the faunal constraints and magnetostratigraphic pattern, the Black Peaks is correlated to the reversed zone below chron 26, to the base of chron 24, or an absolute interval of time ranging from about 62 to 53 Ma. Black Peaks Formation consists of fluviatile mudstones, silts, and sands. The faunal succession of this deposit indicates an age ranging from middle Paleocene (Torrejonian) to early Eocene (Clarkforkian). A minimum of three separately oriented paleomagnetic samples were collected from each of 53 sites in the type and one reference section. Depending upon pilot studies and lithology, in the laboratory the paleomagnetic specimens were treated with either AF or thermal demagnetization (at, respectively, a minimum regime of 25 mT or 200° and 400°C), which appeared to isolate the characteristic component of magnetization. The magnetic polarity zonation is predominantly reversed punctuated by several normal intervals. Based on the faunal constraints and magnetostratigraphic pattern, the Black Peaks is correlated to the reversed zone below chron 26, to the base of chron 24, or an absolute interval of time ranging from about 62 to 53 Ma. Previous hypotheses that the Javelina-Black Peaks and Black Peaks-Hannold Hill lithological boundaries approximate, respectively, the Cretaceous-Paleocene and Paleocene-Eocene boundaries, need to be revised in light of the present study. INTRODUCTION The Black Peaks Formation of Big Bend National Park, Texas, consists of continental sedimentary deposits containing several sig- nificant Paleocene and early Eocene faunas. The geologic history of this formation is im- portant because it is the only Paleocene sedimentary rock unit found in the Trans- Pecos region, and it also contains the south- ernmost occurrence of large Paleocene mam- malian faunas so far discovered in North America (Schiebout 1974, 1980). The purpose of this report is to present the chronology of the Black Peaks Formation by the establish- ment of a magnetic polarity stratigraphy for this unit. On a broader scale, comparisons will then be made with other roughly contem- poraneous faunas which will provide a better understanding of early Tertiary biostratig- raphy and paleobiogeography. 1 Manuscript received November 18, 1982; re- vised May 13, 1983. 2 Present address: Core Labs, 7501 Stemmons Frwy., Box 47547, Dallas, TX 75247. CURTIS Department of Geosciences, The University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona 85721 Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of California, Berkeley, California 94720 ABSTRACT Magnetostratigraphic and 40K - 40Ar data on a 2300 m thick sequence of continental sediments at Puerta de Corral Quemado in Catamarca Province, NW Argentina permit calibration of land mammal faunas of late Tertiary (Huayquerian and Montehermosan) age. The sequence represents (from oldest to youngest) the Chiquimil A, Araucanense, and Corral Quemado Formations. Paleomagnetic samples were collected from 99 stratigraphic levels. Strong-field thermomagnetic and isothermal remanent magnetization experiments indicate that the dominant ferrimagnetic mineral is magnetite. Progressive alternating-field (AF) and themal demagnetization of the natural remanent magnetism (NRM) demonstrates that AF demagnetization to 20 mT peak field is sufficient to isolate the primary NRM which is of depositional origin. The resulting paleomagnetic data provide a well-defined magnetic polarity zonation, although sampling is less dense in the upper half of the section. 40K -40Ar data obtained from mineral separates of four tuffs within the section allow reliable age determinations for those levels. Stratigraphic nomenclature of the late Ter- tiary sediments at Puerta de Corral Quemado and Chiquimil has had a confused history as reviewed by Marshall and Patterson (1981, pp. 14-15) and Bossi and Palma (1982, fig. 1). We follow the terminology used by Riggs and Patterson (1939) because it is the one which appears most frequently in paleontological literature. Second-order events such as these may reflect major, long-sustained shifts in local hydrologic regimen or changes in source area provenance. Schumm (1977, p. 330) defines third-order fluvial cycles as those related to geomorphic thresholds, or step-functions. A definitive cri- teria for a third-order fluvial cycle is the de- velopment of channeling in fluvial deposits. The channel sand/overbank couplet that Allen (1965) defines as the basic fluvial cycle unit would thus be third-order. In the Siwalik sys- tem such third-order fluvial cycles have a 104-105 years periodicity. Lastly, Schumm (1977, p. 330) cites storm and seasonal events as the cause of fourth- order fluvial cycles. In the overbank deposits of the Siwaliks system stratified clays, silts, and sands are frequently intermixed with paleosol horizons. These deposits are gener- ally attributed to seasonal or flood events, which would qualify them as fourth-order fluvial cycles. In the Siwalik system such fourth-order cycles would have return pe- riods spanning a wide range, probably 10°- 104 years depending on the space scale and the process involved. SEDIMENTARY PETROLOGY

In Pakistan and northwest India, the Miocene-Pleistocene equivalent of these sed- iments is generally called the Siwalik Group (fig. 1). In Pakistan the basal sand unit of the Siwalik Group is variously called the Kamlial or Murree Formation. A silty redbed unit usually overlies this basal sand and is desig- nated the Chinji Formation. Together the Kamlial and Chinji Formations are calle

It is noteworthy that the Lower and Middle Siwaliks are analogous fining-upward se- quences, one following the other on a time scale of 106 years. A much smaller-scale fea- ture of Siwalik sedimentation is the cyclic de- position of graded beds, collectively known as fluvial cycles. The frequency and interpre- tation of these larger and smaller cycles will be addressed later in this paper. The base of the section is the base of the Kamlial formation, which occurs near the top of Chron 17 (18.3 m.y.). The Kamlial-Chinji formation boundary occurs in the middle of Chron 15 (14.3 m.y.), the Chinji-Nagri boundary near the bottom of Chron 10 (10.8 m.y.), and the Nagri-Dhok Pathan boundary at the Chron 8-9 boundary (8.5 m.y.). The Siwalik deposits near Chinji Village consist of four distinct classes of fluvial cycles, each with a characteristic periodicity: a first

urth order of 10°- 104 years. The river system responsible for Siwalik sedimentation flowed from west to east and had properties much like the modern Ganges River system. Sedimentation rates in the Chinji Village area increased gradually through time, going from 0.12 mm/yr in the Lower Siwaliks to 0.30 mm/yr in the Middle Siwaliks. At about 11 m.y. blue-green hornblendes suddenly appear in abundance in channel sands. The appearance of these hornblendes, accompanied with accelerated sedimentation, is the effect of uplift in the source area, specifically the Nanga Parbat region. The modern Chinji Village area is no longer a depositional site, but instead is involved in overthrusting, uplift, and erosion. As the Indian Plate has drifted north during the past 18 m.y., the Chinji Village area has been gradually transformed from a subdued karst topography into a major depositional center for Himalayan sediments and finally back into a sediment source area to complete a sedimentary cycle that has spanned some 20 m.y. uller (1978) found that the range of unblocking temperatures (Tub'S) of an experimentally-induced SRM extended beyond 500°C. The shock magnetization pro- cess thus appears to be controlled by the coercivity of the magnetite grains present, af- fecting only the low-coercivity fraction, but partially activating the entire Tub spectrum. However, because Tub's depend upon coer- civity as well as upon grain volume and time (Neel 1955), most of the SRM also resides in the low Tub fraction and is therefore vulner- able to thermal perturbations. Thermal reset- ting of magnetic remanence at low to moder- ate temperatures (well below the Curie temperature) depends strongly on the time available for the magnetization to equilibrate with an ambient field. In natural events (im- pact or otherwise) where large volumes of rock are heated by shock, cooling proceeds slowly, and time may be available for significant thermal resetting of the SRM. Varne & Rubenach (1972) argue from petrological evi- dence that the island rocks are similar to those formed at accreting plate margins. This boun- dary lies within the Macquarie Ridge Complex which extends as an arcuate system of ridges and troughs from the Macquarie triple junction between the Indian, Pacific and Antarctic plates (shown by Sykes (1970) to be near Lat. 62°S, Long. 160°E) to the Alpine fault at the south of New Zealand. The success of the bedding correction in reducing the 95 percent confidence radius from 25° to 12° argues that the lavas were laid roughly horizontally and the dykes injected roughly vertically. Specimens were heated twice to each temperature, cooled and remeasured; the first of each pair of heatings was conducted in zero magnetic field (achieved with a surrounding coil system; McElhinny et al., 1971), and the second in the ambient laboratory magnetic field (60 <"T). The first heating and cooling cycle removes a portion of the natural remanent magnetisation (NRM), and the second replaces it with a laboratory thermoremanent magnetisation (TRM). Since TRM is proportional to the magnetic field in which it is acquired, com- parisons between the NRM and laboratory TRM pro- vide estimates of ancient geomagnetic field strength. Measurements are usually presented as NRM-TRM diagrams, in which the partial NRM remaining after heating t

pe equal to the ratio between NRM and TRM, which would be the same as the ratio between the ancient and laboratory magnetic fields (Nagata et al., 1963; Coe, 1967a). In practice, however, the points are scattered by experimental error, weathering, changes in the magnetic minerals during the laboratory heat- ings, and other forms of non-ideal behaviour (Coe, 19676). Therefore, lines are fitted to those points which appear to lie on a straight line; the NRM is generally excluded because of the possible presence of viscous components, and high-temperature points that deviate are also excluded. The direction for basalt at Mt Schank differs from that of Mt Gambier by several degrees, and indicates that the two volcanoes differ in age, probably by three centuries or more. Directions for both volcanoes are much shallower than the present-day geomagnetic direction at the locality. The geology has been described by Sheard (1978) and may be summarised as follows. There were two separate periods of erup- tion, each with a distinctive style. Period one began explosively with ash and country rock ejection, and ended passively with basalt lava extrusion. Following a time break, long enough to allow complete solidifi- cation of the lava flows (at least two years), the second eruptive period commenced (Fig. 2). Mount Schank rises abruptly from the surrounding plain 14 km south of Mt Gambier (Fig. lb). It is a complex maar-cone structure, where the combina- tion of abundant groundwater and small magma source produced an edifice smaller than Mt Gambier. Initially lava flowed westward from a NW trending line or fissure, marked now by a line of small scoria cones (Fig. 3). More explosive activity followed, with the development of a larger scoria cone and small maar at the southern end of the fissure. A large hybrid maar-cone structure, straddling the small maar and almost obliterating the larger scoria cone, marks the end of activity at Mt Schank (Joyce, 1971; Sheard, 1980). ROBERTSON Department of Physics University of Auckland Private Bag Auckland, New Zealand* Abstract A paleomagnetic study has been made of 99 specimens from 11 sites in the recent basalt lavas of Rangitoto Island. The measured natural remanent magnetisation (NRM) had a formation mean direction of 1.9°E, -62.1°, (X95 = 2.6°; ther­ mal cleaning changed the formation mean NRM direction only slightly to 0.2°E, -61. 7°, Ct9 5 = 1.8°. The densities, magnetisations, and magnetic sus­ ceptibilities measured for each site are recorded. Since Konigsberger's Qn ratio is large in every case, it follows that the aeromagnetic total force anomaly is symmetrical about the geographic meridian. Paleomagnetic declinations, at each site, when compared with historically recorded declinations of the geomagnetic field, confirm the dating results previously obtained by the 14C method; that is, Rangitoto was an active volcano between A.D. 850 and A.D. 1800, with a maximum of activity between A.D. 1200 and A.D. 1500. It is inferred that near Auckland the geomagnetic field has changed direction at approximately 2.87 X 10-2 deg/year eastwards, and changed little in inclina­ tion, during the last 1000 years. A dark, densely welded lenticulite containing large black fiamme is at the base, grading upwards to a grey, densely welded ignimbrite containing randomly oriented black pumice clasts «150 mm) at the top. The basallenticulite is best exposed in a reference section within the Matahana Basin, 2.3 km northeast of the type section (N85/573884). The ignimbrite is generally deficient in crystals; phenocrysts include plagioclase, magnetite, hyper­ sthene, calcium-poor clinopyroxene, and horn­ blende. Quartz is confined to the upper third of the flow. Small rhyolite xenoliths are common. The full extent of the ignimbrite is unknown as much was removed by erosion prior to eruption of the Marshall Ignimbrite, and present outcrop is restricted by the cover of younger pyroclastics and alluvium. However, it does extend south from the Matahana Basin towards the Guthrie Graben where it is presumably downthrown by northwest-trending faults. RAHOPAKA IGNIMBRITE (ri) (new name) The type section of the Rahopaka Ignimbrite is a 300 m roadside section extending east from the Pukerimu- Tikorangi Roads junction at N85/546873 to 550874. The ignimbrite is flat lying, 60+ m thick, and overlies pyroclastic deposits. At the type section the lower contact of the Rahopaka Ignimbrite is obscured by a slip, but above this it is grey-brown, crystal rich, and densely welded near the base. The degree of welding decreases towards the top where it is generally only moderately welded. Phenocrysts in decreasing order of abundance are plagioclase, quartz, hornblende, magnetite, and hypersthene. The visible abundance of green-brown hornblende is the most characteristic mineralogical feature of this ignimbrite. The ignimbrite base is also exposed on Rusa Road, 1.8 km from the Tikorangi-Rusa Roads junction (N85/582851) where it is poorly welded and again overlies pyroclastics with a basal 70 mm thick pumice ash zone. In this region the base has a transgressive red colouration, variable in thickness, and attributed to post-depositional oxidation during cooling of the ignimbrite flow. Xenoliths of Rahopaka Ignimbrite in basaltic scoria on Harry Johnson Road (N85/584854) indicate that, like the Tikorangi Ignimbrite, the

MAMAKU IGNIMBRITE (mk) This was named by Martin (1961) who defined the type locality as the gorge of the Mangarewa Stream at the Kaharoa- Tauranga Road Bridge (N67/646258). Briggs (1973) gives a generalised profile through the ignimbrite at the type area. It crops out in the southwest of the Matahana Basin where it separates into a number of flows. Here it is a crystal-rich quartzose ignimbrite which, apart from a thin zone of dense welding, is generally poorly welded. Phenocrysts consist of plagioclase, quartz, hypersthene, magnetite, and trace amounts of hornblende. ABSTRACT Lord Howe Island is the eroded remnant of a large shield volcano. Tholeiitic lavas of the North Ridge Basalt comprise the main shield building phase and were erupted about 6.9 Ma ago. The Boat Harbour Breccia probably formed within the throat of the volcano and, together with the North Ridge Basalt, is intruded by numerous basaltic dykes, which grade into a cone sheet complex near the main vent. Large scale collapse of the summit area of the volcano produced a caldera which was filled rapidly by lavas of the Mount Lidgbird Basalt some 6.4 Ma ago, bringing to a close the volcanic history of Lord Howe Island

pecially at the southern end of Salmon Beach. Virtually no outcrops are found on the higher parts of Intermediate Hill, above about 100 m altitude, but it is inferred from the distribution of outcrops of the breccia that it underlies the whole of this area, as shown on the map (Fig. 3). Nevertheless, a number of massive smooth outcrops of weathered, structureless, basaltic rock that are not breccia occur on the ridge running from Rocky Point toward the summit of Intermediate Hill, especially at an altitude of about 100 m. Similar out- crops are found at an altitude of about 60 to 80 m on the NE slopes of Intermediate Hill above Rocky Run. In thin section these rocks are seen to be exten- sively altered with development of chlorite, epidote and calcite, although clearly originally of basaltic composition. No lava flow tops or bottoms were found, and thus possibly the rocks may be intrusive bodies. The origin of the Boat Harbour Breccia is prob- lematical, but we suggest that it was formed mainly by explosive volcanism within the central vent region of the volcano, and therefore may be an agglomerate. No contact was observed between the Boat Har- bour Breccia and North Ridge Basalt, but it must lie in the waist of the island between Blinky Beach and Prince William Henry Bay. Thus it is not pos

dipping approximately 25° to the SW, probably a talus deposit originating from the caldera wall. In turn this conglomerate is overlapped by the fiatlying lavas of the Mount Lidgbird Basalt. On the northern flanks of Mount Lidgbird the cal- dera margin can be rocated only approximately, owing to lack of outcrop. However, in a prominent buttress on the NW flanks of Mount Lidgbird (Fig. 9), at an elevation of about 150 m, caldera-filling lavas and interbedded conglomerate lap onto a complex of basaltic dykes and fragmental material, possibly erupted along or adjacent to the caldera boundary fault, as at Red Point. Game (1970) has given detailed petrographic de- scriptions of the Mount Lidgbird Basalt, and he pre- sented much data on their chemistry and mineralogy. The basalts range from strongly porphyritic types to almost aphyric types. Moderately phyric lavas are most common with olivine as phenocrysts, but plagio- clase and clinopyroxene occur also. The rocks typi- cally have an intergranular groundmass, commonly exhibiting flow texture, and consisting of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, olivine (commonly iddingsitised), iron oxide and varying proportions (up to 25 percent) of mesostasis, which is poorly crystallised to glassy. The mesostasis is turbid with alteration and is partly re- placed i

also be classified as transitional. Thus the main shield-building lavas (North Ridge Basalt) are tholeiitic basalts, the dykes are olivine basalts, and the caldera-filling lavas (Mount Lidg- bird Basalt) are transitional to alkali olivine basalts and hawaiites. This change in composition with time from tholeiitic to alkaline is commonly observed in oceanic volcanoes, for example in many of the Hawaiian volcanoes (Macdonald & Katsura, 1964) and in Reunion (Upton & Wadsworth, 1972). GEOCHRONOLOGY Methods Samples were collected from many of the lavas and dykes for possible potassium-argon (K-Ar) age deter- mination. Each sample was examined in thin section, but very few were holocrystalline and free of altera- tion. Nevertheless, some samples met the minimum criteria for dating as whole rocks. Each sample was crushed to a fragment size of —1 mm + 0.5 mm, an aliquant was taken and crushed to less than 0.15 mm, and this representative sample was reserved for potas- sium analysis by flame photometry. The coarser material was used for analysis of argon by fusing a weighed amount, usually 5 to 20 g, in a high vacuum extraction line, mixing the evolved gases with an 38Ar tracer; following purification, the argon was isotopi- cally analysed in an AEI MS-10 mass spectrometer, as described previously (

port- able, gasoline-powered drill, following techniques de- scribed by Collinson et al. (1967). The cores were oriented using a sun compass, by geographic sighting, or by magnetic compass. Normally a minimum of three cores was obtained from each lava, dyke or sheet sampled. Laboratory procedures for measurement of the direction of magnetisation are similar to those de- scribed previously (McElhinny, 1973). Alternating field (AF) demagnetisation procedures were used on all samples, and in some cases thermal demagnetisa- tion was undertaken; these techniques were employed to investigate the stability spectra of the magnetisa- tion components. AF demagnetisation adequately iso- lated the primary magnetisation where only one thermoremanent component was present; these tests were carried out in incremental fields to a peak alter- nating field of 100 mT. Mean directions of magnetisa- tion were calculated at each step, and the results listed in Tables 3 to 6 were selected on the basis of the demagnetisation level that gave the smallest scat- ter of directions. Where the magnetisation was clearly complex, vector analysis, in conjunction with thermal demagnetisation, was carried out. This procedure per- mitted elucidation of the complex magnetisation his- tory of the Boat Harbour Breccia. North Ridge Basa

Dykes and sheets Oriented samples were collected from each of 32 dykes and sheets, well-distributed through the North Ridge Basalt in the northern half of the island and in the Boat Harbour Breccia. Seven of the sites were in basaltic sheets (dips < 45°) on the western shores of Boat Harbour; although the sheets are considered to be just dykes with a shallower dip, results from them will be considered separately, at least initially. With few exceptions, samples from individual intru- sives yielded well-grouped directions subsequent to AF demagnetisation (Table 4). Only at one site does the within-site scatter exceed 18° at the 95 percent confidence level. Iron, in various mineralogical forms, is widely dis- tributed throughout the Hawkesbury Sandstone (Osborne, 1948; Hunt et al., 1977). In fresh bedrock (usually drill core samples) siderite is the most abun- dant iron-bearing mineral, but in surface outcrop it rarely occurs (Standard, 1964, 1969). In fact, surface outcrop is generally depleted in all iron minerals, but they are locally abundant, occurring as concentrations of goethite and/or haematite, with occasional mag- hemite (Hunt et al., 197*7). Concentrations of both goethite (which is unsuitable for palaeomagnetic work) and haematite occur in the Hawkesbury Sand- stone on the monocline, but maghemite was not de- tected. Palaeomagnetism affords a method of establishing the time at which this haematite was introduced into the Hawkesbury Sandstone. The haematite occurs most commonly as a pore-filling cement in the open, sandy quartz fabrics of the Hawkesbury Sandstone 'sheet facies' (Conaghan & Jones, 1975). Palaeomagnetism affords a method of establishing the time at which this haematite was introduced into the Hawkesbury Sandstone. Individual crystals of haematite acquire a permanent chemical remanent magnetisation (CRM) consistent with the direction of the Earth's field, when a critical or minimum 'blocking' volume is reached (Haigh, 1958). This CRM can be measured and compared with the Aus- tralian Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP), to give the age of the haematite introduction. The cali- bration of the APWP depends on combined K-Ar dating and palaeomagnetic studies (Wellman et al., 1969), although relative dates may be inferred from palaeomagnetic poles alone, if their physical age dif- ferences are sufficient. Traditional interpretations of the Blue Mountains portion of the southeastern Australian highland and the Lapstone Monocline, placed uplift/folding in the late Pliocene/early Pleistocene, during the Kosciusko Uplift (or Kosciusko Stage). This age of folding—• first suggested by Andrews (1910, 1934) and re- iterated by many others, including Browne (1969) and Scheibner (1976)—was based on a Davisian interpretation of eastern Australian landforms. Osborne (1948) suggested that the fold may be con- siderably older, but only more recently, with the advent of the K-Ar isotopic dating method and the determination of the physical ages of many basalts throughout eastern Australia, has there been any real emphasis on the antiquity of the southeastern Aus- tralian highland. The bulk of these dates was pro- vided by Wellman & McDougall (1974) who drew attention to the great age of many of the surfaces on which basalts are found in highland areas adjacent, to the Blue Mountains. Branagan (1975) proposed that folding of the Lap- stone Monocline could be related to the opening of the Tasman Sea, 60 to 80 Ma ago, and hence sug- gested a late Cretaceous to early Tertiary age for the monocline. By comparing components of stable magnetization measured in oriented samples of the dykes with the catalogue of palaeomagnetic data for late Precambrian and early Palaeozoic rock sequences and units obtained from independent studies, it is possible to place constraints on the age of dolerite intrusion. This strategy of using palaeomagnetism as an indirect dating technique is most successful where a detailed record of apparent polar wander (APW) is available. For the particular time span under consideration, studies by McWilliams and McElhinny (1980), Kirschvink (1978), Klootwijk (1980), Embleton and Giddings (1974) and Goleby (1980) have provided the necessary detail. Routine procedures (Collinson et al 1967), including the use of a sun compass, were followed in the collection and preparation of oriented rock specimens, nominally 25 mm diameter and 22 mm high. Partial thermal demagnetisation to measure the blocking temperature spectra was carried out in a large, non- magnetic furnace again screened from the influence of the Earth's magnetic field with a custom built ten-coil field control system. Field values were maintained with feed-back in the range + 5 nT during experimental work. The single most noticeable feature of the natural remanent magnetizations (NRM's) is the ubiquitous influence of lightning induced magnetic overprints; or isothermal remanent magnetizations (IRM's). The direction of the NRM measured in one specimen from each independently oriented drill- core sample is plotted on a stereographic (equal angle) projection in Fig. 2. Despite the dispersing effect of the IRM, the NRM's do display a preferred orientation sub-parallel with (i) the direction of the Earth's present field (PF, Fig. 2) at the sampling locality and/or with (ii) the model dipole field direction (DP, which is nearby to PF, Fig. 2) for the respective latitude of sampling, presumably due to viscous remanent magnetization (VRM). PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS Fifty-one independently oriented samples from nine dykes were collected using a portable field drill. The sampling sites are shown in Fig. 1. Routine procedures (Collinson et al 1967), including the use of a sun compass, were followed in the collection and preparation of oriented rock specimens, nominally 25 mm diameter and 22 mm high. The measurement of magnetic remanence was accomplished using a DIGICO complete results fluxgate magnetometer. Experiments to test the stability of remanence to alternating field (AF) demagnetization as a measure of the coercive force spectra were carried out with a SCHONSTEDT GSD-1 demagnetizer, screened from the Earth's magnetic field with /x-metal, and with a custom built three-axis AF demagnetizer housed in specially constructed field coils similar to those described by McElhinny et al (1970). Partial thermal demagnetisation to measure the blocking temperature spectra was carried out in a large, non- magnetic furnace again screened from the influence of the Earth's magnetic field with a custom built ten-coil field control system. Schmidt CSIRO Division of Mineral Physics and Mineralogy, PO Box 136, North Ryde, NSW 2113, Australia. Samples from nine dolerite dykes that outcrop in the Northampton Block, Western Australia, have been analysed to investigate the palaeomagnetic constraints that may be placed on the timing of magmatic events in relation to the widespread lead and zinc mineralization in the Northampton Mineral Field. The palaeomagnetic directions are consistent with a group of pole positions obtained from independent studies of formations of latest Precambrian and very earliest Cambrian age. The pole for the dykes lies at latitude 47.1°S, longitude 317.3°E (A95=7.9°). A comparison with the palaeomagnetic catalogue suggests that the dykes cannot be younger. Results from radiometric studies yield ages for two dykes at 550 Ma and a third dyke at 750 Ma. Located in the Little Ajo Mountains of western Pima county (Fig. 1), the deposit at Ajo is typical of the province in its association with a Late Cretaceous-early Tertiary (Laramide) intrusion. The intrusion is relatively iso- lated from other mineralized plutons in the region and lies within a wide area of mid-Tertiary volcanics. The intrusion at Ajo is hosted by a thick sequence of volcanic rocks, and the associated orebody is similar to the porphyry copper-gold-type deposit of the Lone Star mining district in Graham county, Arizona, de- scribed by Langton and Williams (1982). One of the first copper districts to be mined by Americans after the Gadsden Purchase of 1853, the deposit at Ajo has produced approximately 2.5 million tons of copper, with gold and molybdenum by-products, between 1917 and 1984 when production was suspended. The first comprehensive study of the geologic framework of the Ajo mining district was that of Gil- luly (1946). He concluded that the orebody is asso- ciated with the displaced apex of a large pluton ex- posed by deeper erosion to the west. Detailed grid mapping of this large pluton by Wadsworth (1968) made possible its subdivision into multiple intrusive phases an

ossible its subdivision into multiple intrusive phases and showed petrologic similarities between a portion of the pluton and the ore zone, supporting Gilluly's interpretation. K-Ar ages of 63 to 65 m.y. (McDowell, 1971) confirmed the Laramide age of the mineralized rocks but indicated an age of approxi- mately 20 m.y. for the pluton to the west (Table 1). This discrepancy was ascribed by McDowell (1971) to a younger episode of alteration in the western plu- ton. Cox et al. (1981) described highly saline fluid inclusions in igneous quartz grains from the western pluton which also contain chalcopyrite daughter min- erals. This reinforced the hypothesis that hydrother- mal fluids had evolved from the crystallizing pluton and formed the porphyry copper deposit now faulted down to the east. Cox and Ohta (1984) remapped the pluton, revising Wadsworth's (1968) work, and noted sodic-calcic alteration assemblages like those recog- nized in the deep zones of the Yerington porphyry copper deposit in Nevada (Carten, 1979). carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: the porphyry copper province centered in southeastern Arizona. Located in the Little Ajo Mountains of western Pima county (Fig. 1), the deposit at Ajo is typical of the province in its association with a Late Cretaceous-early Tertiary (Laramide) intrusion. The intrusion is relatively iso- lated from other mineralized plutons in the region and lies within a wide area of mid-Tertiary volcanics. The intrusion at Ajo is hosted by a thick sequence of volcanic rocks, and the associated orebody is similar to the porphyry copper-gold-type deposit of the Lone Star mining district in Graham county, Arizona, de- scribed by Langton and Williams (1982). One of the first copper districts to be mined by Americans after the Gadsden Purchase of 1853, the deposit at Ajo has produced approximately 2.5 million tons of copper, with gold and molybdenum by-products, between 1917 and 1984 when production was suspended. The first comprehensive study of the geologic framework of the Ajo mining district was that of Gil- luly (1946). He concluded that the orebody is asso- ciated with the displaced apex of a large pluton ex- posed by deeper erosion to the west. Detailed grid mapping of this large pluton by Wadsworth (1968) made possible its subdivision into multiple intrusive phases an

ossible its subdivision into multiple intrusive phases and showed petrologic similarities between a portion of the pluton and the ore zone, supporting Gilluly's interpretation. K-Ar ages of 63 to 65 m.y. (McDowell, 1971) confirmed the Laramide age of the mineralized rocks but indicated an age of approxi- mately 20 m.y. for the pluton to the west (Table 1). This discrepancy was ascribed by McDowell (1971) to a younger episode of alteration in the western plu- ton. Cox et al. (1981) described highly saline fluid inclusions in igneous quartz grains from the western pluton which also contain chalcopyrite daughter min- erals. This reinforced the hypothesis that hydrother- mal fluids had evolved from the crystallizing pluton and formed the porphyry copper deposit now faulted down to the east. Cox and Ohta (1984) remapped the pluton, revising Wadsworth's (1968) work, and noted sodic-calcic alteration assemblages like those recog- nized in the deep zones of the Yerington porphyry copper deposit in Nevada (Carten, 1979). This ob- servation also supported a cogenetic relationship be- tween the pluton and the orebody. However, this re- lationship recently has been put in doubt by unpub- lished U-Pb data (L. T. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: d deviation and is based on experience with replicated analyses in the Menlo Park laboratories This report presents the results of both palcomag- netic and geochronologic studies. The K-Ar geochro- nology was undertaken to test the hypothesis that the western pluton and the eastern mineralized intrusion are cogenetic. Because intrusive rocks lack conven- tional indicators of the palcohorizontal, palcomag- netic measurements were made on samples from plu- tonic and related igneous rocks of the Ajo mining dis- trict to estimte the structural disturbance these rocks have undergone since emplacement. Upon cooling below their magnetic blocking temperatures, igneous rocks acquire a remanent magnetization parallel to the ambient geomagnetic field that is stable over geo- logic time. Stable remanent magnetizations may also be acquired by rocks subject to subblocking-temper- ature chemical alteration. The direction of the geo- magnetic field at Ajo for the time the plutonic and related igneous rocks cooled and became magnetic can be calculated from palcomagnetic directions for contemporaneous rocks at undisturbed sites else- where in North America. Thus, comparisons of pa- lcomagnetic directions from igneous rocks in the Ajo district with the expected Late Cretaceous-early Ter- tiary and middle Tertiary geomagnetic-field directions provide initial postcooling horizontal datums for these rock units. Introduction THE Ajo mining district is part of the porphyry copper province centered in southeastern Arizona. Located in the Little Ajo Mountains of western Pima county (Fig. 1), the deposit at Ajo is typical of the province in its association with a Late Cretaceous-early Tertiary (Laramide) intrusion. The intrusion is relatively iso- lated from other mineralized plutons in the region and lies within a wide area of mid-Tertiary volcanics. The intrusion at Ajo is hosted by a thick sequence of volc

Exposed to the east of this diorite is quartz monzodiorite and medium- to coarse- grained granodiorite. ll, J.G., 1982. Complete remagnetization of some Permian dykes from western Norway induced during burial/uplift. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 30: 415—421. Stable paleomagnetic directions in four basaltic dykes and in some associated Caledonian metamorphic rocks define high-latitude, Mesozoic paleomagnetic pole positions which are not compatible with the K—Ar age of —250 My determined for the dykes. A monotonic increase of —~ 40% occurs in the potassium content of samples taken across a dyke 32 cm wide. This is accompanied by only a 1—2% variation in the K—Ar age of the samples, suggesting the absence of any significant level of initial argon. Titanomagnetite grains having bulk compositions around x = 0.6 have suffered extensive low-temperature alteration, forming assemblages of ferri-rutile granules in a matrix of pure magnetite. The complete remagnetisation of both the dykes and the associated country rocks is probably an expression of a VRM acquired at elevated temperatures (150—500°C) at the emplacement depth of the dykes. A stable remanent magnetisa- tion was locked-in during uplift of the area, probably related to the Kimmerian basin development in the adjacent North Sea and the epeirogenic uplift of western Fennoscandia. 1. ite as determined by the new method of analysis. INTRODUCTION Azimuthally unoriented vertical cores comprise most of the material available for paleomagnetic measurements from many oceanic plates. The paleomagnetic data ob- tained from such cores consist of a set of inclination values of known sequence but unknown spacing in time. The objective in analyzing these data is to determine the paleolatitude of the sampling site. If paleomagnetic data are available from widely separated sites on the same plate and if both the paleolatitude and its associated confidence limits are known for each site, the data may be combined to yield a paleopole for the plate and an ellipse of 95% confidence [Gordon and Cox, 1980]. The coordinates of the paleopole and the orientation, size, and ellipticity of the confidence ellipse depend not only on the site coordi- nates and paleocolatitudes but also on the magnitude of the confidence intervals. Therefore the need has arisen for a method of analysis that yields an accurate estimate of confidence limits for paleolatitude data from azimuthally unoriented vertical cores. Rather than a succession of central volcanic activities with only one or two centres being active at any one time (as depicted by Grunevald), parallel development of a number of centres is indicated. Rather than an island-wide basement being established early on, it now appears that the exposed basement to each centre is not significantly older than much of the superstructure. Thus there are areas of basement, previously regarded as Eocene, which now appear to be Plio- Pleistocene. Moreover, some longer-range lateral correlations on the basis of petrographic type are now seen to be invalid. The results will be discussed regionally and generally in order of increasing age, though this is not practicable in every case. The active centre of Mt Pelee, designated Quaternary by Grunevald has only a single whole rock age determination of 0.4 + 0.2 Ma (Andreieff et al. 1976). Volcanics of the Piton Mont Conil area have yielded a whole rock age of 0.6 Ma from a plagioclase-phyric andesite (Nagle et al. 1976) and 2.63 Ma from a hornblende separate. It is important, then, to ascertain the maximum age of material which can be assigned to that plate. By chance, the first radiometric age to be published from the Lesser Antilles area was 140 Ma (Fink 1970; Mattinson, Fink & Hopson 1973) but it is now clear that this is an isolated occurrence and in any case doubt has recently been cast upon its validity (Dinkelman & Brown 1977). Marine geological studies of the Venezuelan Basin indicate that it has been an area of pelagic deposition since a period of extensive flood basalt emission about 80 Ma ago (Donnelly 1975). The Greater Antilles have a stratigraphic history extending well back into the Mesozoic (Khudoley & Meyerhofs 1971). Fossil identifications on the islands of the Lesser Antilles indicate ages of marine sediments as old as early Eocene (Lewis & Robinson 1976). These early Tertiary sediments were deposited on a developing island arc where activity has since ceased, and has been succeeded as the site of volcanism by the Volcanic Caribbees. Abstract: Paleomagnetic samples were collected from a sill and dykes of Ferrar dolerite of the Jurassic age in the Wright Valley, the Allan Hills, the Carapace Nunatak and Mt. Fleming of the McMurdo Sound region. The stability of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of these samples was tested against the alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization, and the hysteresis and thermomagnetic properties were also measured. Concluding Remarks The concl usions to be drawn from the present analysis may be summ arized as follo ws : The samples from the Wright Valley, the Allan Hills and Mt. Fleming have a stable NRM representing the magnetic field at the time of the intrusion of Ferrar dol erite. The stability of the NRM was in ferred from the results of hysteresis analy­ ses, AF demagnetizat ion and thermal demagnetiza tion. On the other hand, the samples from the Carapace N unatak may have both a hard and a soft compo nent of NRM. The main magnetic mineral s consis t of almost pure magnetite in samples from the Wright Valley, Allan Hills (A), and Mt. Fleming, and titanoma gnetite in samples from the Carapace N unatak. The obtained virtual geomagnetic pole pos itions in the Jurassic age are 45.3 °S• 15 2 ° W, 47.0 ° S• l3 3. 2° W, and 68.6 °S• 13 9.5 °W for the Wright Valley, the Allan Hills, and Mt. Fleming respectively. The center of these VGP posit ions, includin g the pre­ vious Jurassic data in Antarctica, is located on the Sou thern Pacific Ocean at 53.9 ° S, 141 .8 °W at present. Abstract: A total of 216 paleomagnetic samples of the Beacon Group (sandstone) were collected from Mt. Circe, Mt. Knobhead, Allan Hills and Mt. Fleming. The respective sedimentary sequences are Pre- or Early-Devonian, Devonian, Permo-Triassic and Triassic. The representative samples were tested for NRM stability against AF and thermal demagnetization, ARM and TRM acquisi­ tion, and AF demagnetization of ARM. The following results were obtained. Introduction Paleo magnetic investigations of the Beacon Group were carried out with the samples collected from the Ferrar Glacier (78°S, 161 °E) by TURNBULL (1959), and from the Wright and Victoria Valleys (77.5°S, l6I.0°E) by BULL et al. (1962). They reached the general conclusion that NRM (Natural Remanent Magnetization) at these sites is parallel to that of indubitably younger dolerite sills (Ferrar dolerite) in spite of a separation of 150 m from the lower boundary of the sill. That is, a large intrusive mass of the Ferrar dolerite nearby caused sufficient heating to raise the Beacon Group to the Curie point and must have been remagnetized in alignment with the ambient geomagnetic field in the Jurassic Age. According to the geological evidence in East Antarctica, the formations ranging in age from Middle Paleozoic to Messozoic were only the Beacon Group (sandstone) in the Transantarctic Mountains and the Prince Charles Mountains of the Lambert Glacier (i.e. RA VICH and FEDOROV, 1977). Therefore, it is very important to carry out an investiga­ tion of the Beacon Group paleomagnetically in order to elucidate the history of Gond­ wanaland, as the East Antarctic plate is probably situated in the center of that region. 2. Received 1992 December 15; in original form 1992 October 20 SUMMARY A palaeomagnetic study has been made of samples collected from Permo-Triassic type sections in the Emei Mountain region of southwest China. No results were obtained from the Lower Permian Qixia Formation limestones or the (Lower)- Upper Permian Maokou Formation limestones. The Upper Permian (Longtanian) Emeishan Basalt Formation shows excellent stability to both alternating field and thermal demagnetization. Results from 24 flows (125 samples) are all of normal polarity, have a positive fold test (Cretaceous or Tertiary folding), and give a pole position at 54.5"N, 254.3"E with dp = 1.8", dm =3.5". The basalts were thus presumably extruded after the end of the Kiaman Reversed Superchron. The overlying Upper Permian Xuanwei Formation of red mudstones and sandstones (Changxingian in age) also shows a positive fold test from N = 12 samples after thermal treatment and has a positive reversals test at level C. In these red sandstones when components are observed directly below and above 600 "C, we have interpreted them according to the classical experiments of Roy & Park (1974) on redbeds from North America. The first component (A) removed on thermal cleaning up to 600 "C is presumed to be a CRM from either magnetite or specular haematite. Each group is made up of a few islands and small islets up to some 20 km*. Since the end of the 19th century, the Bonin Islands have been studied by a number of scientists mainly from a petrological and paleontological point of view. This direction (S45.4 ø, W48 ø) is not consistent with published poles for the Ordovician or Silurian of North America, but rather it is a Late Paleozoic pole more consistent with Permian time. Introduction Recently Monger et al. (1982) subdivided composite Terrane I, essentially the Intermontane Belt of the Canadian Cordillera, into four sub- terranes including the Stikinia subterrane of northcentral British Columbia (Figure 1). Earlier Monger and Irving (1980) reported on paleomagne- tic results from Stikinia. After alternating field (AF) demagnetization in the 30 to 60 mT range and thermal demagnetization in the 500 to 600øC range, they found that the Upper Triassic Takla Group volcanics, the Lower Jurassic Hazelton Group volcanics, and the mid-Cretaceous Axelgold layered gabbro intrusion from Stikinia all have remanence inclinations which indicate that they were formed at about 13 ø more southerly paleolatitudes than their present locations. Thus they concluded that Stikinia has moved northward by about 1300 km since mid-Cretaceous time. In summary, the revised pole for the Topley Intrusions resolves the paleolatitude conflict created by the original data, and thereby simplifies the construction of geotectonic models for Cordilleran evolution. Symons Department of Geology, University of Windsor, Windsor, Ontario, Canada, N9B 3P4 Abstract. The 142 Ma old Jurassic Topley Intrusions are exposed in the middle of the Intermontane Belt or Stikinia subterrane of composite Terrane I of the Canadian Cordillera in central British Columbia. Thermal demagneti- zation at 560øC leads to the isolation of a single stable magnetic component directed at 324'2ø' 54'1ø' 95 = 8'6ø in 17 of the 22 sites. The pole position of 238,2øW, 58.4øN, p = 8.3 ø , a m = 11.8 ø for the component is discordant relative to the North American craton. This position supports previous work in suggesting that Stikinia has been translated northward by 14 + 2 ø or about 1400 km between mid-Cretaceous and pre-Miocene time. It also suggests that the central portion of Stikinia has not been rotated about a vertical axis by a statistically signifi- cant amount whereas minor marginal blocks of the subterrane have been subjected to large and variable amounts of both clockwise and counter- clockwise rotation. As relief is considerable in the region, fresh, unweathered material was readily available. All samples were collected by orienting blocks (independent measurements) in the field using a magnetic compass; standard specimens were pre- pared in the laboratory. We employed a spinner magnetometer, on which was attached a 500 count/ rotation optical shaft encoder. Signal analysis and data acquisition were carried out using an interfaced microprocessor. The instrument has a sensitivity of better than 1 x 10 -4 A/m; this is adequate to resolve almost all significant com- ponents during demagnetization. Orthogonal de- magnetization diagrams and vector subtraction techniques were used to calculate component di- rections. LEADVILLE (CARBONATE) FORMATION AND IMPLICATIONS FOR THE AGE OF SUB-REGIONAL DOLOMITIZATION Robert A. Horton, Jr. and John W. Geissman Department of Geology, Colorado School of Mines Richard J. Tschauder Hecla Mining Company Abstract. The Mississippian Leadville Formation of Central Colorado is dolomitized near the Sawatch Uplift and hosts numerous Pb- Zn-Ag mineral deposits. Paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data from several dolomite types away from centers of Tertiary intrusive activity imply a late Paleozoic (Late Mississippian, ?) age for the dolomitization (e.g., D - 148 o, I = -11 ø, k- 86, 9s = 8.6% N - 3 localities, 31 samples in dolomitized units). The magnetiza- tion is of diagenetic origin and was probably acquired during or soon after dolomitization. Tertiary thermochemical activity has overprinted dolomites close to intrusive centers. Data indicate that limestones removed from igneous activity were also remagnetized at the same time. Introduction and Geologic Setting The nature and origin of the paleomagnetism in carbonate rocks have received considerable attention over the past decade [e.g., Lowrie and Alvarez, 1977; Heller and Channell, 1979; Lowrie and Heller, 1982; McCabe et al., 1983a]. Paleo- magnetic data have constrained the ages of eve

paleomagnetism in carbonate rocks have received considerable attention over the past decade [e.g., Lowrie and Alvarez, 1977; Heller and Channell, 1979; Lowrie and Heller, 1982; McCabe et al., 1983a]. Paleo- magnetic data have constrained the ages of events affecting carbonates, such as regional dolomitization, base metal mineralization, and oxidation [e.g., Wu and Beales, 1981; Shanks et al., 1979; McCabe et al., 1983a; Wisniowiecki et al., 1983; Channell et al., 1982]. It has been shown that the major carriers of the magne- tization may be diagenetic in origin McCabe et al., 1983a,b]. We have examined aspects of the Leadville Formation (Kinderhookean-Osagean) of Central Colorado. The Leadville Formation offers an opportunity to study the relations between diagenesis, regional dolomitization, Tertiary igneous activity, structural deforma- tion, and the magnetization of a stable shelf carbonate. Here, we discuss the paleomagnetism of Early Mississippian limestones and sub- regionally dolomitized equivalents on the flanks of the Sawatch uplift (Figure 1). and the magnetization of a stable shelf carbonate. Here, we discuss the paleomagnetism of Early Mississippian limestones and sub- regionally dolomitized equivalents on the flanks of the Sawatch uplift (Figure 1). The spatial association among pervasively dolomitized Leadville Formation, numerous Pb-Zn-Ag deposits, and Laramide (latest Cretaceous to mid-Tertiary) plutons in the Leadville-Gilman area have led to suggestions that the intrusives were the source of the metals and that hydrothermal fluids were the source of magnesium in the dolomites .g., overall character of the ore deposits, which are found throughout the Leadville Formation, have prompted suggestions that some metals were intro- duced by low-temperature brines in Late  Paleozoic time eVoto, 1983; Tschauder and Landis, 1983; Horton et al., 1983]. Understand- ing the age and origin of dolomitization is important to understanding the Pb-Zn-Ag deposits. This investigation is concerned with paleomagne- tic information bearing on the age of dolomiti- zation. The Copper Mountain intrusions include four bodies: i) the Copper Mountain stock (-12 km 2) has an outer diorite phase with gabbroic zones that grades inwards through monzonite to a perthositic pegmatite core; ii) the Voight stock (-5 km 2) is composed of a similar diorite; iii) the Lost Horse intrusion (4 km2) contains albitized and sausseritized diorite, monzonite and syenite cut by latite to trachyte dikes; and, iv) the Smelter Lake stock comprised of diorite only (Montgomery, 1967). The four bodies give Lower Jurassic minimum K-Ar mineral ages between 191 + 7 and 203 + 9 Ma [Sinclair and White, 1968; Preto et al., 1971; Preto, 1972]. They contain massive nonfoliated rocks except on the west side of the Lost Horse intrusion where extensive shearing and alteration are found near the Boundary Fault. The Copper Mountain intrusions are cut by the 102 + 4 Ma Verde Creek quartz monzonite and by the northerly-trending Mine Dykes of felsite and quartz/feldspar porphyry. The latter are believed to be related to the unconformably overlying Eocene Princeton Group of basic volcanics and clastic sediments [Preto, 1972]. In the laboratory, samples were cored and standard paleomagnetic specimens prepared. Usually 2-3 specimens were cut from a sample, though in some cases shale partings made it impossible to obtain good specimens. Some of the samples were set aside for rock magnetic or dissolu- tion experiments. Specimens were demagnetized in the laboratory using both AF and therma] treatments and measured with an ScT cryogenic magnetometer. Each specimen was demagnetized in stepwise fashion. The demagnetization data were plotted on orthogonal de- magnetization diagrams and the directions of the component magnetizations were determined by vector subtraction (ZijderveId, 1967). To obtain extracts of the magnetic minerals for direct observation, representative Trenton samples were powdered in an alumina-ceramic grinding dish, and the carbonate was dissolved with buffered acetic acid (1.5 M; pH=4.0). The magnetic fraction of the insoluble residue was extracted from a water suspen- sion with a home-built magnetic extractor. Magnetic extracts were studied using scanning electron micro- scopy energy dispersive X-ray analysis and powder X- ray diffraction techniques. Results Demagnetization studies d

The magnetite and its associated remanence appear to have a diagenetic origin. Introduction Sedimentary carbonates of Trentonian age form one of the most widespread rock units in North America. The Trenton Limestone in New York State has been the object of at least two previous paleomag- netic investigations. Graham (1954, 1956) reported well-clustered natural remanent magnetization (NRM) directions that have a mean declination/inclination of ]790/+82 o. McElhinny and Opdyke (]973) resampled the same section at Trenton Falls, New York that was sampled by Graham. They showed that Graham's results, which were obtained without any demagneti- za

ion at Trenton Falls, New York that was sampled by Graham. They showed that Graham's results, which were obtained without any demagneti- zation, are contaminated with a component of rema- nence aligned with the present-day magnetic field. After alternating field (AF) demagnetization they found a mean direction of 173o/+18o. Further, they showed (as had Graham) that the magnetization was acquired after a syndepositional slump but that the minimum and maximum axes of magnetic suscepti- bility anisotropy show a typically sedimentary fabric. They concluded that the magnetization was due to early post-depositional reorientation of the magnetite carrier grains in the ambient Ordovician field. Several factors prompted us to undertake yet another investigation of Trenton paleomagnetism. Recent studies of Paleozoic carbonates from eastern North America (eg. Scotese et al., 1982; McCabe et al., 1983; Wisniowiecki et al., 1983) have demonstrated that some carbonate rock units were chemically re- magnetized during the late Paleozoic by the dia- genetic development of new magnetite. Introduction Sedimentary carbonates of Trentonian age form one of the most widespread rock units in North America. The Trenton Limestone in New York State has been the object of at least two previous paleomag- netic investigations. Graham (1954, 1956) reported well-clustered natural remanent magnetization (NRM) directions that have a mean declination/inclination of ]790/+82 o. McElhinny and Opdyke (]973) resampled the same section at Trenton Falls, New York that was sampled by Graham. They showed that Graham's results, which were obtained without any demagneti- zation, are contaminated with a component of rema- nence aligned with the present-day magnetic field. After alternating field (AF) demagnetization they found a mean direction of 173o/+18o. rized by Barton and Merrill [1983], Creer et al. [1983], coal beds that dip gently basinward have been exposed by erosion. The extensive clinker deposits represent a number of discrete burn events. Up dip, clinker is progressively older, with fission-track ages ranging from less than 0.08 to 0.77 ñ 0.39 my [Coates and Naeser, 1984]. In the northern Powder River Basin, ages are as old as 1.4 my [Jones et al., 1982]. Few reports describe remanence and/or rock magnetic properties of clinker [Krs, 1968; Purucker, written comm., 1980; Watson, 1978]. Discussion The Dunn Point volcanics present surprisingly non-complex and generally univectori al magneti za- tions, with a mean direction of declination/in- clination = 335ø/-61 ø . The fold test constrains the age of mag- netization to pre-Middle Devonian time. Although the remanence is carried by hematite, the flows are inferred to have undergone early oxidation; a primary age of the magnetization is therefore quite likely. Upper Triassic-Lower Jurassic rocks at Quesnel Lake form part of the Quesnel terrane, which was emplaced against the Omineca Belt, part of the North American (paleo-)continental margin, in the late Early Jurassic. Hard magnetizations, which may or may not be primary, were identified in volcanic wackes, but they are poorly grouped. However, removed magnetizations of intermediate unblocking temperatures (200-500øC) and coercivities (30-50 roT) are systematically directed northeast and downward (D=35 ø, I=57 , a95--9 , 5 sites, 22 specimens; paleopole 62N, 15øW, din--13 , dp=10 ø) with respect to present horizontal. We interpret this to be an overprint, acquired after Middle to Late Jurassic folding, as a result of mid-Cretaceous plutonism during the Cretaceous Normal Superchron. The paleopole is compatible with Early to mid- Cretaceous paleopoles from other terranes in the southern Canadian Cordillera, but does not agree with observations from post-Jurassic cratonic rocks. This disagreement indicates that in the mid-Cretaceous these terranes, along with at least part of the Omineca Belt to which they were attached, formed a quasi-rigid super-terra

s not agree with observations from post-Jurassic cratonic rocks. This disagreement indicates that in the mid-Cretaceous these terranes, along with at least part of the Omineca Belt to which they were attached, formed a quasi-rigid super-terrane which was situated about 2000 km farther south than its present position relative to the craton. Introduction In what is now the southern Canadian Cordillera, the first oceanic terrane to be emplaced against the ancient continental margin of western North America (now the Omineca Belt) in the early Mesozoic was Terrane I (Figure 1; Monger et al., 1982; Monger, 1984). Terrane I is a composite of several smaller terranes, one of which is the Quesnel terrane. Paleomagnetic results from the Quesnel terrane are described. The Quesnel terrane, as part of Terrane I, was thrust onto the Omineca Belt in the late Early Jurassic, and together they were deformed, metamorphosed, and intruded by syn- to post- tectonic plutons in the Middle to Late Jurassic (Read and Wheeler, 1976; Archibald et al., 1983; Brown et al., 1985). It is important to note that the rocks in the sampling locality are structurally continuous with the adjacent Omineca Belt, indicating that since the Quesnel terrane was emplaced, there has been no significan

Jurassic, and together they were deformed, metamorphosed, and intruded by syn- to post- tectonic plutons in the Middle to Late Jurassic (Read and Wheeler, 1976; Archibald et al., 1983; Brown et al., 1985). It is important to note that the rocks in the sampling locality are structurally continuous with the adjacent Omineca Belt, indicating that since the Quesnel terrane was emplaced, there has been no significant relative movement between them. Geology At Quesnel Lake (Figure 2; 52.5N, 121.5W) zeolite facies rocks approximately equivalent to the Upper Triassic-Lower Jurassic Nicola Group and Takla Group, comprise mainly alkali basalt lavas and volcaniclastic rocks, and comagmatic Early Jurassic plutons (Morton, 1976). Small intrusions of Cretaceous age are widespread in the area, such as the Bootjack Stock with a whole-rock K-Ar age of 111 _+ 4 Ma (Bailey, 1978). Collections were made in bedded green-grey volcanic wackes, siltstones and mudflow deposits, which are dated by fossils as NorJan and Hettan- gian. Beds dip up to about 70 . Because of the continuity with structures in the Omineca Belt, this folding is correlated with the regional Middle to Late Jurassic deformation. There is no evidence for major post-Jurassic folding. Introduction During historic time, both the amount of secular variation of the Earth's magnetic field (SV) and the magnitude of the nondipole field, whose changes cause most of the historically observed secular variation, have been rather irregularly distributed over the earth's surface [Cox and Doe11, 1964; Doe11 and Cox, 1972]. These features are at the present time of larger magnitude in the Southern Hemisphere than in the Northern Hemisphere and are almost completely lacking in the central Pacific region [Doe11 and Cox, 1962; McWilliams et al., 1981]. As a result of evidence from Hawaii that suggested a sustained interval of low geomagnetic secular variation, analogous studies were conducted elsewhere in the Pacific on the Galapagos [Doe11 and Cox, 1961], on Easter Island [Issacson and Heinrichs, 1976], and in the Society Islands [Duncan, 1975]. These studies showed secular variation consistent with a \"standard\" model of global variation based upon modern dipole and nondipole fields [Cox, 1970; McWilliams et al., 1981] and hence the region of anomalously low secular variation has been constrained to smaller regions of the Pacific. years during the neotectonic period. Le Pichon and Angelier (1979) for instance, consider that major neotectonic movements occur- red in the last 13Ma. According to these authors this movement is at first approximation a 30 ø clockwise rotation of a semi-rigid plate about a pole situated near 40øN; 18øE in the southern Adriatic Sea. A large back-arc distension, up to about 70%, is superimposed to this rotation loc- ally modifying its value which is maximum in the northwestern region and progressively decreases eastward to attain zero near the Anatolian coast. Aegea cannot thus be considered as a rigid plate. The extent of the deformation has led Mercier (1977) and Mercier et al., (1979) to consider Aegea as the plastically deformed edge of the Eurasiatic plate, with movement occurring along slip lines as suggested by Tapponnier (1977). Some of these models (Brunn, 1976; Tapponnier, 1977) assume that the deformation is entirely related to the main Tertiary Alpine phase and is thus completed before the neotectonic period. E. Johnson Department of Geological Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI. 48109 Abstract. A paleomagnetic study of the Late Precambrian Roxbury formation, consisting of extrusives and clastic sediments, has yielded a steeply downward directed and pre-folding charac- teristic magnetization (D/I = 219ø/71 ø , 595 -- 5 ø , k = 311, paleopole at 13øN, 267øE, N = 4 sites), which indicates a significantly higher paleolati- tude (55 ø ) than would be expected if the Boston basin were part of the equatorial North American craton in the latest Precambria and earliest Paleozoic. This characteristic magnetization reveals dual polarities and is further supported by a positive conglomerate test. A ubiquitous post-folding late Paleozoic overprint is present in nine sites (D/I = 183ø/14 ø , 595 = 8 ø , k = 42), with a paleopole at 41øS, 285øE, The pre-folding study addresses the last question, in so far as the Boston basin is concerned. Introduction The Boston basin and much of eastern Massachu- setts form part of the Avalon zone in the Appala- chians, and there is now a general consensus that the Avalon terranes may be exotic (Wilson, 1966; Williams and Hatcher, 1983). They are thought to have joined the North American craton during the Devonian or Carboniferous as a result of the closing of the Iapetus ocean. In order to test and quantify the displacement hypothesis for these terranes, paleomagnetic studies of latest Precambrian and early Paleozoic rocks were initi- ated. Several results have already been published f6r Cape Breton Island in Nova Scotia (Johnson and Van der Voo, 1985, 1986; Van der Voo and Johnson, 1985). Introduction As a result of the indracontinental convergence in Eastern Turkey, most of Turkey moved westward along the North and East Anatolian strike-slip faults. Since at least late Miocene, this motion is accompanied by large scale N-S extension in the Aegean and in Western Turkey with complementary E-W shortening (Tapponnier, 1977; Dewey and eng6r, 1979; Mercier et al., 1979; Le Pichon and Angelier, 1981; Angelier et al., 1981) . In this paper we report paleomagnetic data from northeastern Aegea showing that significant rotations of adjacent coherent blocks about vertical axes and in opposite senses have occurred in this region since at most 20 m.y. Although the data are still incomplete, the complicated rotational pattern in this area is easier to describe in terms of local rotations than in the framework of the general westward movement of the \"Anatolian Plate\" resulting from the Eurasia-Arabia collision (Tapponnier, 1977; Dewey and eng6r, 1979). section_candidates.excerpt: the extensional tectonic regime. Introduction As a result of the indracontinental convergence in Eastern Turkey, most of Turkey moved westward along the North and East Anatolian strike-slip faults. Since at least late Miocene, this motion is accompanied by large scale N-S extension in the Aegean and in Western Turkey with complementary E-W shortening (Tapponnier, 1977; Dewey and eng6r, 1979; Mercier et al., 1979; Le Pichon and Angelier, 1981; Angelier et al., 1981) . In this paper we report paleomagnetic data from northeastern Aegea showing that significant rotations of adjacent coherent blocks about vertical axes and in opposite senses have occurred in this region since at most 20 m.y. Although the data are still incomplete, the complicated rotational pattern in this area is easier to describe in terms of local rotations than in the framework of the general westward movement of the \"Anatolian Plate\" resulting from the Eurasia-Arabia collision (Tapponnier, 1977; Dewey and eng6r, 1979). Geological Setting and Sampling The studied area and the location of the sampling sites are shown in Figure 1. The most striking structural and morphological features of this region re the E-W and NNE trending grabens (McKenzie, 1978; Dewey and eng6r, 1979). Focal m

Focal mechanism solutions obtained from the Alasehir and Gediz grabens, have shown that motion takes place on faults of listric geometry (Eyidoan and Jackson, 1985). The NNE faults are probably partially inherited from Neo-Tethyan-structures while the E-W fault system corresponds to a neotectonic structural direction. The complex pattern of faulting includes numerous other neotectonic faults of various orientations and displacements (Kaya, 1981), most of which are truncated by younger faults of different orientations. Slickensides indicating strike-slip movements in opposite senses and in different directions are also frequently observed in the field.
